All four model families evaluated—LSTM, GRU, CNN and Transformer—learned the input→output mapping from the measured dataset and achieved small test L2 losses (Table 4), confirming that ML is a viable alternative to heavily parameterized physics-first models when the goal is accurate and robust prediction of inverter output behavior. Comparing the architectures on the metrics collected, two clear observations emerge. First, recurrent architectures (LSTM and GRU) produced the lowest test losses (both 2.6e-4) while requiring the least training time overall (196 s and 167 s, respectively). Second, the CNN achieved a similarly good accuracy (test loss 2.8e-4) but required training time similar to the Transformer (≈219–220 s). The Transformer exhibited the largest training loss and test loss in this experimental setup (train 1.1e-4, test 3.2e-4), suggesting that, for the size and variety of our dataset, attention- only architectures offer no clear advantage over simpler recurrent or convolutional structures.
